item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — He is the elephant in the lineup.
Shohei Ohtani’s presence looms large as the Dodgers prepare to open their postseason run with Game 1 of their National League Division Series on Saturday afternoon against the Atlanta Braves.
But what version of the four-time league MVP will be in the lineup on Saturday is a mystery. He has played just eight games in the past month and spoken to the media just once in the past six weeks, so assurances about his health have only come second hand.
But they have come.
“Everything is feeling great physically,” Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes said this week. “The swings, once he came back, overall were in a good place. And using these five days to continue to get reps and feeling good into this series is really important. But feels like he’s in a great spot.”
Ohtani returned for the final five games of the regular season and went 5 for 21 (.238) with just one extra-base hit (a double), one RBI, no runs scored, eight strikeouts and only one walk. But that was enough for Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
“I feel confident that you’re going to see the best version of Shohei of the last two months,” Roberts said, referencing a stretch that saw Ohtani hit .232 with a .745 OPS while compromised by knee and arm injuries.
“I know that’s sort of a low bar given his injury, but I do think that he’s as healthy as he’s been in quite some time, and every day from the training staff, it keeps getting better. So yeah, No. 1 he’ll be a threat being in the lineup, but I do think that the performance piece will be what we’re hoping for.”
Media were not allowed into the Dodgers’ workouts on Tuesday and Wednesday. Ohtani took batting practice on the field each day and also took three at-bats against Yoshinobu Yamamoto during Wednesday’s intrasquad game.
Thursday’s workout was open to the media and Ohtani was nowhere to be seen during batting practice or the intrasquad game that followed.
“His BP outside the last two days was really good,” Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates said during Thursday’s workout. “It was as good as we’ve seen it this year as far as the way the ball was coming off and the way he was getting his move off.
“He looked really good in his BP, in his work. He looks as good as he has as far as that goes. … The ball always comes off his bat hard, but the last two days in particular he was swinging very well.”
Bates said there have been no signs of any physical limitations in Ohtani’s work.
“The physical part he’s kind of moving past that,” Bates said. “Now it’s just getting the timing against different speeds, when he wants to get his move off, that sort of thing – kind of the usual stuff hitters go through as opposed to him navigating trying to achieve the physical components (while injured).”
The expectation is not to have Ohtani – or anyone else in the lineup – at 100% full strength, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said.
“I don’t think anyone is going to be at 100% in October,” Friedman said. “It’s a long, grueling season, and everyone’s on fumes. Our group, the team we’re playing against, everyone is on fumes. And it’s so adrenaline-based that, for me, it’s about each guy just drawing from their experience and having calmness in what they do. And I would bet on our talent to shine through.
“We don’t need anyone to try to do more.”
But they do need “a lot” from Ohtani, Roberts said, in a lineup that has underperformed at times and struggled against the better pitching staffs of the National League.
“We need him to be full strength and do what he does – take good at-bats, take what they give you,” Roberts said. “If they’re going to pitch around you to pitch to Mookie, so be it. And if they make mistakes, then hit it hard.
“Yeah, we need him to be healthy and strong. It certainly helps our offense.”

item.content:encoded:
As the Los Angeles Dodgers prepare to embark on another October with sky-high expectations, there are a few stars who did not end the regular season at 100% health.
Superstars Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman, and flame-throwing relief pitcher Edgardo Henriquez, have perhaps the biggest question marks surrounding them heading into the National League Division Series.
Here's the latest updates on all three players.
Shohei Ohtani Injury Update
Ohtani has dealt with nagging knee and biceps injuries for the majority of the season. His knee eventually shut him down from pitching ahead of the All-Star break, and his biceps injury resulted in the minimum stay on the 15-day IL, returning for a lackluster (5-for-21) final five regular season games.
General manager Brandon Gomes spoke on a Tuesday Zoom call with the media and had an update on the four-time MVP, and how his swing has been looking amid a much-needed break while the wild-card round finishes up.
“Everything is feeling great physically," Gomes said of Ohtani. "The swings, once he came back, overall were in a good place. And using these five days to continue to get reps and feeling good into this series is really important. But feels like he's in a great spot."
Manager Dave Roberts appeared to feel the same about Ohtani, and even went as far as saying that the man who hit just .245 during the second half of the season will still have a stellar postseason.
"I feel confident that you're going to see the best version of Shohei of the last two months," Roberts said. "I know that's sort of a low bar given his injury, but I do think that he's as healthy as he's been in quite some time. And every day from the training staff, it keeps getting better. So yeah, No. 1, he'll be a threat being in the lineup, but I do think that the performance piece will be what we're hoping for."
Freddie Freeman Injury Update
Freeman is no stranger to playing through injury, and has recently been dealing with right knee tendinitis that manifested itself in the form of a .184 batting average in the final 20 games he played of 2026.
"My body feels good,” Freeman said Tuesday. “I think that’s the main thing. I feel like it’s in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that’s been going on the last couple months.”
Freeman was asked to compare his current pain level to past postseasons. Fans remember his heroics in the 2024 World Series —where he would later take home MVP honors — thriving through the Fall Classic despite a sprained ankle and broken rib cartilage.
“A couple of Octobers ago was probably 100 times worse, ailment-wise,” Freeman said. “I truly feel good right now, physically. So it’s on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days, and I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by Saturday.”
Edgardo Henriquez Injury Update
Henriquez put up a 2.85 ERA across 60 innings of work this season, averaging a 100.8 mph fastball (in the 100th percentile among active pitchers), until lower back discomfort landed him on the injured list last month. He was activated off the IL this week.
“He’s trending really well at this point,” Gomes said. “His last live BP went well. He’s responding positively after he throws and isn’t feeling any lingering discomfort. We’ve still got a few steps to go. But if that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster.”
Roberts also made sure to acknowledge how pivotal the off-week was for his fireballer. Due to an excellent track record (a career 2.73 ERA in 86 regular season appearances), he could prove to be a crucial piece this October.
“I think he’s one of those guys that getting the bye has really benefited,” Roberts said. “He’ll throw another live or sim game to some hitters. ... Then he should be ready to go. And given the body of work, what he’s done, the unique skill set could be huge for us, will be huge for us.”

Gabe Smallson is a sportswriter based in Los Angeles with a focus in sports and entertainment content. Gabe has previously worked at Newsweek and Dodgers Nation. He graduated from San Francisco State University in 2020 and received his Masters of Science at the University of Southern California in 2025.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers earned the benefit of a postseason bye and now are reaping the full benefit as the Philadelphia Phillies staved off elimination to force the Atlanta Braves to a winner-take-all Game 3 in their Wild Card Series matchup.
The winner advances to face the Dodgers in the National League Division Series, which begins Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The start for time for Game 1 has not yet been decided as it hinges on whether or not the San Diego Padres or Chicago Cubs reach the NLDS to play the Milwaukee Brewers.
In the meantime, the Dodgers are spending the rest of the week going through workouts and simulated games, much like their approach in 2024 that proved beneficial.
The Dodgers avoiding the Wild Card Series this year has proven beneficial for multiple players dealing with an injury, including Edgardo Henriquez.
He missed the final two weeks because of lower back discomfort but has made steady progress in his recovery and is on track for the NLDS.
“We’ll get him some work this week. He’s trending really well at this point,” Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes said on Tuesday. “His last live BP went well, he’s responding positively after he throws and isn’t feeling any lingering discomfort.
“We’ve still got a few steps to go, but if that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster.”
Elsewhere in the Dodgers bullpen, Edwin Díaz finished the regular season on a high note after returning from a stint on the 15-day injured list because of a neck issue.
“I don’t know if we could have asked much more out of Edwin. I think it was, like, a 50-plus percent strikeout rate when he came back,” Gomes noted. “Felt like each outing was more and more sharp, and looking more like himself.
“Feels like he’s in a great place right now, stuff out of hand is as good as it’s been all year, and we know that he has pitched in the hottest of hot games in the past, and in any role, especially in the postseason. He’s looked great and glad that he’s in the position that he’s in and was able to bounce back after the IL stint.”
Díaz threw five scoreless innings, allowed just one hit and one walk while collecting nine strikeouts across five appearances upon getting activated Sept. 18. While Gomes projected confidence, what may still be different for Díaz is he’s not relied upon as the primary closer.
Even without Shohei Ohtani pitching, the Dodgers are heading into the playoffs with a formidable starting rotation that consists of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. What order they will pitch in has not yet been decided.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said the team would not set their NLDS rotation until Thursday, at which point they would know whether the Braves or Phillies advanced.
“I say that because just trying to figure out opponent and the schedule going forward, not sure about game times and things like that. We’re having conversations but we’re not definitive yet,” Roberts explained.
“I think opponent certainly should matter, could matter. Talking to Mark Prior about where guys are at. To be honest, we could really put all four guys in a hat and run them out there. But I think there is going to be more thought behind it. We don’t need to make a decision right now, so really just trying to be clear and talk through it.”
Last year the Dodgers almost exclusively used Snell (Wild Card, NL Championship Series and World Series) as their Game 1 starter. Ohtani started against the Phillies in the opener of the NLDS.
One change from the 2025 postseason is Glasnow’s first appearance likely won’t come out of the bullpen during the NLDS due in part to a different schedule.

item.content:encoded:
El eficiente relevista cumanés Edgardo Henríquez continúa mejorando de los dolores en la espalda que lo llevaron a la lista de lesionados el pasado 14 de septiembre,
El gerente general de los Dodgers, Brandon Gomes, indicó que Henríquez ha avanzado hasta el punto de enfrentarse a bateadores en una sesión de práctica de bateo en vivo, informó el portal rotoworld.com.
Gomes señaló que la evolución del derecho de 24 años es positiva, lo que parece indicar que formará parte del róster del conjunto de Los Ángeles para la postemporada cuando comiencen su serie divisional de la Liga Nacional este fin de semana.
Leer también: Boston pierde un jugador esencial para lo que resta del comodín
Henríquez, especialista en situaciones de alta presión y dueño de potentes envíos, registró una sólida efectividad de 2.85 y una relación de 71 ponches por 25 bases por bolas en 60 entradas, antes de ingresar a la lista de incapacitados debido a molestias en la zona lumbar.
Cargado de un buen control y de una potente recta, que ha llegado a superar las 100 millas por hora, Henríquez se presenta como una pieza clave en el bullpen de los californianos, que buscan ganar su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva. En criollo en la ronda regular tuvo marca de 4-1 y 2.55 de efectividad con 2 salvados.

item.content:encoded:
One of many things that makes the Los Angeles Dodgers so infuriating to competitors is how lucky they get when it comes to injuries. Over their last three seasons, their pitching staff has been riddled with shoulder inflammation and elbow impingements, and so on — but they always seem to get their key players back exactly when they need them.
They might have lost Blake Treinen in their last series of this season, but he's had a tough year and wasn't a lock for the postseason roster anyway. The real concern was for Edgardo Henriquez, who's been missing since September 14 with lower back discomfort.
Henriquez was officially activated from the IL on Tuesday, but his status ahead of the NLDS still seemed touch-and-go, given how fresh off injury he'll be with zero runway.
There are still boxes he has to check, but Dodgers GM Brandon Gomes said on Tuesday that he's trending the right direction. Katie Woo reported, "should he come out of all bye-week activities (live hitters, sim games, etc), he'll be on the NLDS roster."
The back end of the Dodgers' bullpen has no clear hierarchy right now, so Henriquez would be a welcome addition for later innings.
Edgardo Henriquez trending positively toward returning for Dodgers' NLDS
It's hard to guess what Dave Roberts' trust tree might look like heading into October. Tanner Scott, Edwin Díaz, and Tanner Scott are the obvious closing options, but Scott posted a 4.15 ERA in September, Díaz showed signs of life after his IL stint but still isn't truly trustworthy, and there's no telling if Sasaki will turn back into the lights-out closer he became last season.
The Dodgers used Henriquez as early as the third and as a late as extra innings over the course of the regular season, but he picked up two saves in nine games finished this year. His ability to throw 100+ MPH with regularity is his greatest asset, as long as he can control his pitches.
He was trending toward a more regular eighth- or ninth-inning role before he got hurt, as the Dodgers had to go with closers by committee with Díaz's absences and Scott struggling a little more. Henriquez has been effective anywhere between the seventh and ninth, with just a .191 batting average and .553 OPS against.
The Dodgers' bullpen being as shaky as it still is, the onus will be on the starters (again) to go as deep into games as possible, but Henriquez's presence should add a little more assurance.

item.content:encoded:
While eight teams battle it out to see who will advance to the Division Series, the Dodgers are among four teams using this time off to prepare for October baseball.
After winning an even 100 games in the regular season, the Dodgers secured a first-round bye and will await the winner of the NL Wild Card matchup between the Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies. While the Dodgers continue to add the finishing touches to their postseason roster, there are some lingering questions as to which players will be a part of the team's depth chart.
21-year-old outfielder Josue De Paula made his presence known while filling in for the then-injured Shohei Ohtani, slashing .323/.500/.581 across 42 plate appearances before he was sent down to Triple-A Oklahoma City. Sonja Chen of MLB.com believes that both De Paula and utility man Hyeseong Kim can make an impact on the postseason roster, with the former being relegated to pinch-hit opportunities due to his lack of big-league experience in the outfield.
Of course, De Paula is capable of playing the corner outfield, but we only saw him play six innings in left as a Dodger. And given how important defense is in the postseason, I doubt we will see him in the field unless it's an emergency.
The month of September has given Shohei Ohtani plenty of time to prepare for his third consecutive postseason run with the Dodgers. The Dodgers still have another three days to prepare for the NLDS, and Ohtani is using this time to get his swing in the right place, per Chen.
"Everything is feeling great physically," general manager Brandon Gomes said on a Zoom call with the media on Tuesday. "The swings, once he came back, overall were in a good place. And using these five days to continue to get reps and feeling good into this series is really important. But feels like he's in a great spot."
Freddie Freeman had his power zapped in the second half of the regular season, hitting just one home run while posting a slugging percentage of .339. Freeman dealt with patellar tendonitis in his right knee, but entering the NLDS, he said that he's feeling a lot better, reports Jack Harris of the California Post.
"I truly feel good right now, physically," Freeman said on Tuesday, during a video conference with reporters ahead of the Dodgers' first pre-National League Division Series bye week workout. "So it's on me now to figure out the mechanics of the swing in the next five days. And I have all the confidence in myself that I will figure that out by [Game 1 on] Saturday."

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers to get ‘huge impact’ with key reliever on track for NLDS return
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris

And come the start of their postseason trek on Saturday, the team might be adding another key arm back to the group. item.content:encoded:
Over the last two months of the regular season, no team had a more productive bullpen than the Dodgers.
And come the start of their postseason trek on Saturday, the team might be adding another key arm back to the group.
General manager Brandon Gomes announced on Tuesday that the club expects to have hard-throwing right-handed reliever Edgardo Henriquez available for its National League Division Series, an encouraging development after Henriquez missed the final couple weeks of the regular season with a strain in his back.
Prior to getting hurt, Henriquez was emerging as one of the top arms in the Dodgers’ resurgent relief corps (which led all MLB bullpens in August and September with 4.3 combined wins above replacement, according to Fangraphs, and ranked fourth in that stretch in combined ERA at 3.20).
A 24-year-old former prospect who has started to routinely eclipse 103 mph with his fastball, Henriquez ranked fourth among the team’s relievers (minimum 20 appearances) with a 2.85 ERA this season. He also struck out 70 batters in 60 total innings and converted each of the ninth-inning save opportunities he received.
Henriquez had hit his stride in August and early September, allowing just one run in a 17-game stretch that featured 25 strikeouts and only two walks and seven hits allowed.
However, after giving up two runs in a Sept. 13 appearance in Miami against the Marlins, he went on the IL with his back injury –– one that initially cast doubt on his postseason availability.
Luckily for the Dodgers, Henriquez’s status has improved since then. He resumed a throwing during the team’s final regular-season homestand. He recently completed a session of live batting practice without feeling any lingering discomfort. And while Gomes said “we still got a few steps to go” before Henriquez gets the green light to return, every indication is that he should be available for the club’s best-of-five NLDS.
“If that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster,” Gomes said.
“Given the body of work, what he’s done, the unique skill set, that could be huge for us,” manager Dave Roberts added, before correcting himself: “Will be huge for us.”
Indeed, Henriquez would figure to occupy a high-leverage spot in the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen. He gives them not only a trustworthy right-hander option –– along with Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart and the recently resurgent Edwin Díaz –– but also one of the biggest fastballs in the game.
Henriquez’s 100.7 mph average fastball velocity ranked second among MLB pitchers this season, behind only star Padres closer Mason Miller. The team’s next-hardest thrower is Sasaki, whose heater averaged only 97.9 mph this year (though could increase in the playoffs as he shifts to a bullpen role).
Last October, Henriquez was a mixed bag in the playoffs. In two of his appearances (Game 1 of the wild card series and Game 5 of the World Series), he failed to record an out while allowing a hit and two walks in both outings. But in the other (Game 3 of the World Series), he pitched two scoreless frames in the team’s marathon 18-inning win, becoming an unsung hero in their Fall Classic triumph.
This time, Henriquez is set for a prominent role, assuming he gets through one more session of live batting practice OK.
“[He would make a] huge impact,” Roberts said. “I think he’s one of those guys that getting the bye has really benefited.”

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez is “trending really well,” according to general manager Brandon Gomes, and he is looking likely to be on the NLDS roster.
Henriquez is still on the injured list with a lower back injury, which shut him down for the last two weeks of the regular season.
Edgardo Henriquez injury status
When speaking to the media, including Dodgers Nation, on Tuesday, September 29th, Gomes said Henriquez threw a live batting practice session against hitters, and it went well.
Henriquez also has additional activities lined up during the bye week to clear up, including simulated games and more live batting sessions.
If he clears the remaining checkmarks, Henriquez will be ready for the NLDS, per Gomes.
“We’ve still got a few steps to go, but if all that goes well, the expectation is he will be on the roster,” the general manager said.
What will Henriquez’s role be with the bullpen?
Before he got hurt, Henriquez was a set-up man for the Dodgers, and he was also a budding closer for the team thanks to his consistency.
Tanner Scott is prone to home runs, while Edwin Diaz was in a spiral, which helped Henriquez emerge as the most consistent relief pitcher.
Over the last few weeks, Scott has been steady, while Diaz has rebuilt himself from the ground up. Additionally, Roki Sasaki moved into the bullpen, leading the Dodgers into the postseason with plenty of candidates to close, Henriquez among them.
“Obviously we’ve had a lot of talent over the years,” manager Dave Roberts said. “But as far as sitting here today at the end of the season, it’s as good of shape as we’ve ever been in with the bullpen.
“That could change in a day, in a game, as we all know. But right now, feel really good about everyone out there.”
Roberts is known for making bullpen decisions based on feel in the postseason, and depending on how Henriquez looks coming back, he may close or perhaps settle into a middle relief role.
Luckily, the Dodgers have bullpen options, which hasn’t been the case for a while.

item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers have lost this gamble once before. But that won’t stop them from placing the same wager again.
Rather than take every precaution to ensure Shohei Ohtani doesn’t worsen the injuries to his right arm and left knee, the Dodgers will prioritize giving him at-bats to get him ready for the playoffs.
Ohtani is expected to be activated from the 15-day injured list Wednesday, and manager Dave Roberts said the plan is for him to play in every one of the five games that remain in the regular season.
“He’ll need those live at-bats,” Roberts said.
This feels reckless — and unnecessarily risky, especially when considering what happened the last time the Dodgers were in this position, just earlier this month.
Ohtani was experiencing discomfort in his arm and knee. The Dodgers downplayed the severity of his injuries, with general manager Brandon Gomes claiming the physical problems weren’t responsible for his hitting slump and shouldn’t require him to be placed on the IL.
So much for that.
Roberts described Ohtani as being “pain-free” Sunday, but acknowledged he was still experiencing “discomfort you can play through.” Certain levels of discomfort can be tolerated — until they can’t be, of course. That’s been the story of Ohtani’s season.
When Ohtani started feeling pain in his knee, he insisted he could pitch through it. Until he couldn’t.
When he started to be affected in the batter’s box by the throbbing in his arm and knee, he claimed he could play it. Until he couldn’t.
Roberts said Ohtani’s condition has improved over the last two weeks. But Roberts also didn’t claim Ohtani was completely healthy.
“Is he 100%?” Roberts said. “Probably not.”
In other words, what bothered Ohtani when he landed on the IL still bothers him, just not as much.
This is a problem.
What happened earlier this month showed that if Ohtani plays too many games with these particular injuries, he will reach a point where he won’t even be able to take the field.
Why not give Ohtani every other game off? Will playing five more regular-season games instead of three make that much of a difference? Because the question isn’t whether Ohtani can make it through the next five games. The question is how much closer these games will push him to the point of no return.
The objective should be to make sure Ohtani is available in some capacity throughout the entire postseason, not only at the start of it. If he has to be gradually work his way into form over the playoffs, so be it.
Ohtani would almost certainly reject such cautious thinking. He doesn’t like half-measures. Ohtani takes big swings without much regard to the consequences.
So, if he’s going to use the final week of the regular season to prepare for the playoffs, he’ll probably do so with visions of being an impact player. He doesn’t want a Kirk Gibson moment; he wants to be Mr. October.
Before he went on the IL, Ohtani offered a realistic assessment of his health, saying he didn’t expect to be at 100% between now and the end of the season. But he said he believed he could overcome his physical problems by making adjustments to his swing.
“With some creativity, I think I can make up for what’s not right,” Ohtani said in Japanese. “Another way to say it is that it’s an opportunity to create new ways to compete.”
At the time, that meant learning how to hit with one arm and one leg.
The Dodgers let him, and Ohtani ended up on the IL.
Once again, it sounds as if Ohtani is determined to squeeze in as many at-bats as possible, and once again, it sounds as if the Dodgers will let him try.
This approach has significant upside — and downside, too.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers figuring out how to score runs without Shohei Ohtani
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez

item.content:encoded:
Super Mario ran into a mushroom. Popeye devoured a can of spinach.
The Dodgers are scoring runs in bunches again.
Say what you want to say about the quality of opposition or small sample size, but the numbers are the numbers.
Ninety-seven runs in their first 17 games of September.
Nineteen home runs in their last nine games, including five in their 8-2 win over the Giants on Friday night.
With a little more than a week remaining in the regular season, the Dodgers are finally starting to resemble the team they were expected to be.
Even without Shohei Ohtani.
The Dodgers doing this with Ohtani on the 15-day injured list is the most promising aspect of their recent offensive resurgence.
Because they will likely have to do something like this to give themselves a chance to complete their three-peat.
Manager Dave Roberts reported Ohtani was “in a good spot” as a result of “a really productive last three to four to five days,” but the reality is that the Dodgers have no credibility on this subject whatsoever.
Remember when general manager Brandon Gomes said earlier this month that Ohtani might pitch again this season? Or when Gomes said “nothing has indicated” Ohtani would have to be placed on the IL the day after a game in which he was shaking his arm and looking as if he was hitting on one leg?
Knowing Ohtani, he will be in the Dodgers’ lineup when the playoffs start, but his presence will be more a reflection of his willpower than of his health. The Dodgers can’t count on him to produce, at least not with any consistency.
Which is why it was important that Mookie Betts homered twice on Friday night.
Or that Max Muncy, Kyle Tucker and Will Smith also went deep.
Or that Ohtani’s replacement at designated hitter, 21-year-old rookie Josue De Paula, scored the run that tied the game in the fifth inning and doubled in the go-ahead run in the sixth.
“It’s a high-floor talent level,” Roberts said. “I just like the way we’re taking better team at-bats and making up for not having Shohei in there.”
The Dodgers have scored an average of 5.71 runs per game this month, an improvement from their average of 4.89 through Aug. 31.
They are doing what Betts previously called on them to do, to build momentum in September that can be taken into October.
“We just gotta keep playing good ball and want to keep going through the end of the season,” Betts said. “We don’t want any letups. We don’t want to try and turn anything on once the postseason starts. We just want to play good ball, and we want that to be our identity.”
Betts has played a major role in that, batting .333 with seven home runs and 23 RBIs over his last 25 games.
He isn’t the only player on a hot streak.
Tucker is batting .438 with five homers and 11 RBIs in his last nine games. Teoscar Hernandez is hitting .362 with three homers, three doubles and a triple this month.
De Paula has shown advanced plate discipline, as he’s registered an on-base percentage of .448 in his first eight major league games. He’s walked eight times in 29 plate appearances and struck out only twice.
“Nothing too different, to be honest,” De Paula said when asked to compare the major leagues to Double- A.
He continued, “I always felt like I was a good hitter. I know these pitchers know how to execute a little bit better and stuff, but I know I’m up for the challenge.”
Roberts said De Paula has played his way into consideration for a spot on the playoff roster. What Roberts didn’t say was that De Paula could be an insurance policy at DH in case Ohtani’s body doesn’t hold up over the postseason.
Roberts has insisted that when Ohtani returns, he will be slotted right back into the leadoff spot, but Betts could give the manager something to think about.
Twice in the last week, Roberts batted Betts at the top of the lineup, and Betts was a combined 5-for-8 in those games.
Of hitting first, Betts said, “It’s fun and kind of feels home. But there’s a guy named Shohei that needs to be up there to get us going.”
Roberts also made no effort to downplay Ohtani’s importance.
“Obviously, we’re a better team with him,” Roberts said. “But it is nice to see that there hasn’t been a drop-off with him not in the lineup.”
The Dodgers can’t expect Ohtani to shoulder as much of the offensive burden as he did last year in the playoffs, when he was responsible for eight of their 24 home runs.
When the team wasn’t hitting in July or August, that would have sounded like a death sentence. Now, a more balanced offense sounds like a possibility — or at least more possible than it was earlier in the season.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have not seen enough evidence to put Shohei Ohtani on the injured list, general manager Brandon Gomes said Thursday, adding that an extended absence had not been discussed as the club continued evaluating him day to day.
“Nothing has indicated that it should be an IL at this point,” Gomes said.
Gomes said the Dodgers would prefer to avoid losing the four-time MVP from the lineup for roughly 10 days. He also questioned whether a prescribed period of rest would necessarily resolve the physical issues Ohtani has been managing.
“It really hasn’t even, you know, been something that we discussed,” Gomes said of the longer absence.
Why Shohei Ohtani has not gone on the injured list
Asked whether a longer break could help, Gomes acknowledged that it might, but said the team could not be certain of a benefit or identify a set number of days that would solve the problem. His preference was to continue checking how Ohtani felt and consider individual days off as needed.
That explanation came amid visible signs of discomfort at the plate. Gomes acknowledged the arm shaking from the previous night as something the Dodgers needed to monitor closely. He did not announce a new diagnosis or say Ohtani’s symptoms had disappeared.
Gomes said he had not yet seen Ohtani that day at the time of his remarks. The next steps would depend on further conversations and how Ohtani responded physically.
Gomes stops short of tying the slump to physical issues
Gomes was pressed on whether Ohtani’s offensive struggles and lingering symptoms were connected. He said it was difficult to separate physical factors from the normal fluctuations of a baseball season and did not believe the Dodgers could definitively establish that connection.
He described Ohtani as a “victim of his own greatness,” suggesting that the expectations created by his usual production amplify the attention on a difficult stretch. Gomes said Ohtani continued following his routine and putting in the work.
Those comments offered a different emphasis from Dave Roberts’ assessment after Wednesday’s game. Roberts said he saw wincing, arm shaking and compensation in Ohtani’s swing, and subsequently said the symptoms had not been improving.
Roberts’ observations concerned what he was seeing physically. Gomes’ response concerned whether the club could conclusively attribute Ohtani’s offensive results to those issues. Neither assessment amounted to an announcement that Ohtani would go on the injured list.
Pitching innings remain valuable, but not at any cost
Gomes said the Dodgers were also continuing to weigh a possible pitching return against the need to protect Ohtani’s offensive contribution.
“Any Sho innings are really valuable,” Gomes said. “But if it comes at a cost, then you make that decision.”
He said the club still had time to see how Ohtani responded and threw before deciding whether continuing the pitching effort made sense. He did not announce a shutdown or a date for another pitching appearance.
Gomes also described Ohtani as willing to communicate with the organization. He said their interests were aligned around putting Ohtani, and in turn the team, in the best position to succeed.
For now, the Dodgers’ stated approach remained day-to-day evaluation, not a commitment to uninterrupted playing time or a scheduled extended break.

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the California Post's weekly Dodgers recap, where we review the week that was, hand out very official awards and take stock of the state of the season.
PLAYER OF THE WEEK
Kyle Tucker (12-for-29 since Sept. 9; triple shy of the cycle on Thursday)
Off the bat, it appeared history was afoot.
Already on Thursday afternoon, Kyle Tucker had kicked his slow late-season turnaround into a suddenly more hopeful gear, hitting a two-run home run in the first, an RBI double in the second and a single that aided a three-run rally in the fourth.
Now, standing at the plate just a triple shy of the cycle in the eighth, he laced a line drive that made the feat feel possible.
With yet another squared-up swing, the $240 million slugger shot a ball into the left-center field gap. As two Reds outfielders converged on it, the entire Dodgers dugout rose in anticipation.
Alas, the 11th cycle in Dodgers history would have to wait.
The Reds turned a clean relay play. Tucker wisely — although, somewhat disappointingly, given the lopsided score — pulled up at second. And on the bench, all his teammates could do was razz him by mimicking send signs with their arms helplessly waving.
"I tried my best, but I don't think I was gonna get there," he told SportsNet LA afterward. "I probably would've been thrown out halfway."
Oh, well.
For this year's Dodgers, Tucker's 4-for-5, three-RBI game was still hugely encouraging, continuing what is now a weeklong surge in which the four-time All-Star has finally looked like himself.
Even before this stretch, the Dodgers committed to keeping Tucker as a key part of their lineup.
They hoped a breakthrough he made with his mechanics could salvage something from an otherwise disastrous debut campaign with the team.
Well, in his last eight games, Tucker has batted .414 with seven extra-base knocks, 10 RBIs and more walks (five) than strikeouts (four).
He has hit five home runs in his last 13 games, after collecting just 11 in his first 132 games this year.
It is the version of Tucker that the Dodgers will need in the playoffs, especially with fellow left-handed bats like Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman battling ongoing injuries.
After a season that once seemed so lost, signs of revival have arrived just in time.
PITCHERS OF THE WEEK
Tarik Skubal and Yoshinobu Yamamoto (seven scoreless innings from each)
We are going with a tandem honor this week, from a pair of pitchers who will likely have the biggest influence on the Dodgers' World Series chances.
With Blake Snell battling a groin injury, and Tyler Glasnow entering a Friday start having recently regressed in his return from the injured list, the Dodgers' rotation doesn't feel quite as formidable as it once did.
Then again, if Skubal and Yamamoto keep pitching like they did this week — when they spun consecutive scoreless seven-inning outings in Cincinnati — those other question marks might not feel so daunting.
Both pitchers have sterling postseason track records: Yamamoto with a 7-1 record and 2.25 ERA in 10 playoff outings (including last year's World Series heroics) and Skubal with a 2-1 record and 2.04 ERA in six October appearances of his own (all with the Tigers the last two years).
Either could anchor a pitching staff on their own capable of making a run to the Fall Classic.
Together, they give the Dodgers arguably the best 1-2 punch in the majors. This week, they delivered the club's first pair of back-to-back scoreless seven-inning outings since 2022 when Tyler Anderson and Clayton Kershaw did it.
Granted, dominating the Reds in mid-September is not the same as producing gems in the playoffs.
But with so many other concerns mounting at the moment, Skubal and Yamamoto at least represent a pillar of potential pitching excellence to lean on, one that could compensate for other shortcomings in the Dodgers' three-peat bid.
PROSPECT OF THE WEEK
The entire Dodgers' minor-league system
The Dodgers' big-league club hasn't been the only one popping bottles in beer-soaked clubhouse celebrations recently.
This year, all four of the organization's minor-league affiliates also clinched places in their respective playoffs, with Triple-A Oklahoma City completing the quad-fecta by winning the second-half title in the Pacific Coast League on Wednesday.
It marks the first time the Dodgers have had four affiliates make the playoffs since 2019 (and that year included their now-defunct rookie-ball outpost in Ogden, Utah).
It's also the latest reminder about the strength of depth they boast in their highly touted farm system.
"I know people don't care about minor-league win percentages, but we kind of do," Dodgers general manager Brandon Gomes told the California Post earlier this season. "I think it's a good proxy of how well your farm system is performing and how to understand what it takes to win."
Three of the club's affiliates have already been eliminated, with Double-A Tulsa, High-A Great Lakes and Single-A Ontario all losing in their division championship series.
OKC, meanwhile, will begin its postseason push next week in the best-of-three PCL Championship Series against the Athletics' Las Vegas affiliate. If they win that, they will remain in Vegas for the Triple-A National Championship Game against the winner of the International League.
QUESTION OF THE WEEK
Who should Dodgers hope to see in the first round of the playoffs?
With the NL West crown secured, the Dodgers still have work to do over the season's final nine games.
Given their injury problems, they've never needed a first-round bye so badly.
The good news: They remain four games up on the Braves for the NL's No. 2 seed, with their magic number down to six for securing passage straight to the NL Division Series.
And though they remain two games back of the Brewers for the best record in the majors — and home-field advantage throughout the playoffs — conventional wisdom in recent weeks has suggested that the playoff through the postseason might be better from the 2-seed anyway.
Now, however, the NL playoff field is getting muddied, with the red-hot Padres sitting just one game back of the Cubs and Phillies.
So, who should Dodgers fans root to see in a potential first-round matchup? Well, it depends on what kind of matchup you think suits the Dodgers best.
The Cubs and Phillies had seemed like tougher draws than the Braves or Padres, thanks to Chicago's deep and homer-happy lineup and the Phillies' powerhouse starting rotation trio.
But this week, Philadelphia lost one of its star pitchers, Jesús Luzardo, to a shoulder injury that has put his playoff availability in doubt. The Cubs, meanwhile, have seen their offense cool off and still face questions with an unimposing starting rotation.
The Braves have their own flaws (they've been a middle-of-the-pack offense since the All-Star break) but still boast Chris Sale at the top of their rotation.
The Padres, on the other hand, are making a familiar late-season surge and have a habit of playing the Dodgers tough in the playoffs.
It will all make for a fascinating final few days of scoreboard watching, with a slew of new postseason permutations now on the table.
The Dodgers, of course, won't be overly worried about who they might square off against. Their focus is on continuing to play a better brand of all-around baseball — and making sure they avoid the best-of-three wild-card round.

item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani may play again this season, according to baseball operations president Andrew Friedman.
While taking a ton of champagne and celebrating a 13th National League title in 14 years, Friedman took a question about Ohtani and his outlook.
“He’s doing well,” Friedman said. “He’s progressing well. I expect him back in the regular season.”
Ohtani was not with the team in Cincinnati to celebrate the NL West title; instead, he was in Los Angeles continuing his rehabilitation on his injured right bicep and his left knee.
According to manager Dave Roberts, Ohtani had a day off on Wednesday, though he did hit off a tee and will do some hitting from a coach’s pitches at some point this week.
“There’s no pain. He’s doing everything he needs to do,” Roberts said. “I still don’t know when [the] time to return to play is. But everything that I hear is really positive.”
Does Ohtani need to play in the regular season?
The Dodgers will play Ohtani in the postseason, regardless of whether he plays in the regular season again, general manager Brandon Gomes said, focusing on how he feels rather than his season participation.
“The most important thing is that he’s healthy and in good shape. Whether it’s during the regular season or after that, as long as he’s fully prepared and ready to go, we’re fine with it,” Gomes said, per Japanese reporter Masaya Kotani.
Ohtani has mentioned in the past that he doesn’t get better from playing; rather, rest is the best medicine.
If that is the case and Ohtani can sharpen up a bit with batting practice, sitting him may ensure the Dodgers see the best version of their best player.
Ideally, fans get to see him take some swings over the next week and look better than he did before landing on the injured list.
In his last plate appearances, Ohtani struggled to rotate his body into swings and generate full extension.
He looked to wince after swings, suffering from visible pain in his right arm.
If he can swing fully and tune up his vision for the postseason, it is worth rolling him out, but the Dodgers will err on the side of caution no matter what.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani may not even need to return in the regular season to play in the postseason.
Japanese reporter Masaya Kotani asked general manager Brandon Gomes whether Ohtani could return in the postseason after missing the rest of the regular season.
“Yeah, I think that’s a possibility,” Gomes said, according to the translation of Kotani’s tweet. “The most important thing is that he’s healthy and in good shape. Whether it’s during the regular season or after that, as long as he’s fully prepared and ready to go, we’re fine with it.”
Ohtani is currently sitting out with a bicep injury from pitching, which has landed him on the injured list, and is also dealing with left soreness, according to manager Dave Roberts.
What is the next step for Shohei Ohtani?
Ohtani spent some time hitting off a tee on Tuesday at Dodger Stadium, his first taste of baseball action since landing on the injured list.
The Japanese star “felt good” after the session, per the Dodgers skipper.
The Dodgers will likely have him continue swinging the bat gradually, and they will monitor him every step of the way to see whether a regular-season activation is possible.
According to Roberts, Ohtani spent Wednesday resting back in Los Angeles, not engaging in baseball activities.
The Dodgers have one more game in Cincinnati left for Thursday, Sept. 17th, before they travel to Los Angeles for two home stands against the Giants and Padres.
During their time in LA, with the coaching staff available to evaluate Ohtani, they’ll have a clearer picture of his outlook before the season ends.
Compared to what was previously assumed, Ohtani’s regular-season participation matters much less if he plays in the postseason no matter what.
